title: Framing & Error Control
summary: See how the data link layer carves a raw bitstream into discrete frames, detects transmission errors, and paces senders against receivers.

slides.sectionTitle: From raw bits to trustworthy frames
slides.markdown: The physical layer hands the data link layer an undifferentiated stream of bits — no boundaries, no guarantee they arrived intact. This layer's job is to carve that stream into **frames** and catch (most) transmission errors before handing clean data up to the network layer.

A physical link only delivers a continuous stream of bits — there's no inherent "start" or "end" marker. **Framing** is the job of marking where one unit of data begins and ends, so the receiver knows what chunk to hand up to the network layer.

Without framing, a receiver has no way to tell "these 1500 bytes are one packet" from "these are the tail of one packet and the head of the next" — every data link protocol has to solve this before anything else works.

Three classic approaches solve framing:

- **Byte counting** — prefix the frame with its length. Simple, but a corrupted length field derails every frame after.
- **Byte stuffing** — use marker bytes for start/end, escaping any occurrence of that marker inside the data.
- **Bit stuffing** — use a flag bit pattern (e.g. `01111110`), inserting an extra `0` after five consecutive `1`s so the flag can't appear by accident.

Ethernet mostly sidesteps this with a preamble plus length field, but stuffing still shows up in HDLC and PPP.

Once a frame's boundaries are known, the receiver needs to know if its bits got corrupted. Three techniques, in increasing strength:

- **Parity bit** — one extra bit makes the total 1-count even (or odd). Catches single-bit errors, misses even numbers of flips.
- **Checksum** — sum the data in fixed blocks, send the sum along. Cheap, catches many errors, misses some patterns.
- **CRC** — treat data as a polynomial, divide by a fixed generator; the remainder is the check value. Far stronger at burst errors — the Ethernet standard.

CRC appends the data with zeros, divides by the generator polynomial using binary XOR, and keeps the remainder as the check value:

![Binary division of a message by a generator polynomial to compute a CRC remainder](assets/crc-division-example.svg)

The receiver repeats the same division on the received frame (data + CRC); a zero remainder means "no detected error" — not "definitely correct," just "no error this check catches."

assets.alt: Binary division of a message by a generator polynomial to compute a CRC remainder

slides.markdown:
The data link layer usually **detects** errors and asks for a retransmission, rather than **correcting** them on the spot. Correction (FEC) needs extra redundant bits sent with every frame regardless of whether an error occurs — a constant tax.

Detect-and-retransmit only pays that cost when an error happens, the default on links where errors are rare (wired Ethernet). Lossy, high-latency links (satellite) flip this calculus, since a retransmit costs an expensive round trip.

Flow control paces a fast sender against a slow receiver, independent of error handling:

- **Stop-and-wait** — send one frame, wait for an ack, send the next. Simple but wastes time on every frame, especially over high-latency links.
- **Sliding window** — send several frames before an ack, up to a window size; slide it forward as acks arrive. Better utilization, needs sequence numbers and buffering.

TCP reuses this exact idea at the transport layer — a recurring pattern, not a one-off trick.

| | Retransmission (ARQ) | Forward Error Correction (FEC) |
|---|---|---|
| Extra bits sent | Only a small check value per frame | Substantial redundant data, every frame |
| Recovery cost | A full round-trip if an error occurs | None — corrected immediately, no round-trip |
| Best fit | Low-latency, low-error links (LAN, fiber) | High-latency or lossy links (satellite, deep space, live streaming) |

**How to decide:** if a retransmit round-trip is cheap, ARQ wins on efficiency; if a round-trip is expensive or impossible (one-way broadcast, extreme latency), pay the constant FEC tax instead.

slides.sectionTitle: A passing checksum isn't a correctness guarantee
slides.subTitle: CRC can miss the errors it wasn't designed to catch
slides.markdown:
A common mistake is treating a passing CRC or checksum as proof the data arrived correct. It isn't — CRC is designed to reliably catch specific error patterns (all single-bit errors, all burst errors up to its check length, most others), not literally every possible corruption.

A sufficiently unlucky combination of bit flips can produce the exact same remainder as the original data — rare, but not impossible. That's why layers above still add their own integrity checks where correctness genuinely matters (e.g. TLS's message authentication codes) rather than relying on link-layer CRC alone.
